title: A Deported NRI, a Missing Brother, and a Fake Canada Immigration Racket. Ab Hoga Hisaab Knows Exactly What Scares the Diaspora.
excerpt: Streaming free on Amazon MX Player from June 18, this Punjab-set revenge thriller turns the migration dream into a nightmare — and stars Sanjay Kapoor as the man you'll love to hate.
body:
The trailer opens on a note of dread, and it earns it. A quiet, recently deported man steps back into his Punjab hometown carrying the particular shame the diaspora knows intimately — the dream that didn't take, the visa that ran out, the return nobody back home will let you forget. Then his younger brother vanishes somewhere on the road to Canada, and Ab Hoga Hisaab stops being a homecoming story and becomes something far darker.

Produced by Arré Studio and streaming free on Amazon MX Player from June 18, this is the rare crime thriller that builds its terror not from a serial killer or a haunted house, but from the most ordinary aspiration in any NRI household: the desire to get out, get abroad, and build something better. That it lands free, on a platform reachable on Prime Video, Fire TV, JioTV and Airtel Xstream, only sharpens the point — this is a story aimed straight at the families living the fantasy it dismantles.

"Gunahon ka aur karmon ka… Ab Hoga Hisaab." — The series' haunting refrain
**"It's the horror of the WhatsApp forward your aunt sends with the caption "be careful."

What makes the show worth your weekend is the cast playing in a register we don't often see them in."**

Here's the premise, and it's a gut-punch. Shaheer Sheikh plays Bobby Manocha, the elder brother whose entire identity is wrapped up in sending his sibling Bunty abroad. Bunty — played by Avinash Mishra, making a confident OTT debut — is the dreamer, the one who's supposed to make it. The brothers scrape together the money, chase the opportunity, and head for Canada. And then, somewhere in the machinery of it all, Bunty disappears. What Bobby uncovers is not bad luck but a sinister human-trafficking syndicate dressed up as a Canada immigration network — the kind of operation that preys on exactly the hope these two brothers were running on.

If that scenario sounds uncomfortably plausible, that's because it is. The series is loosely inspired by true events, and any NRI who has watched the headlines about the "donkey route," deportation flights, and immigration consultancies that turned out to be fronts will feel the floor drop out. This isn't fantasy horror. It's the horror of the WhatsApp forward your aunt sends with the caption "be careful."

What makes the show worth your weekend is the cast playing in a register we don't often see them in. Sanjay Kapoor is the revelation here as Goldy Sekhon — a ruthless power broker who believes in striking before time runs out, delivering ominous lines with the unhurried menace of a man who has never once been told no. Kapoor has spent a career being underrated; on this evidence, the villain era suits him beautifully. Mouni Roy, fresh off her well-received turn in Salakaar, plays Kamna, described as a sharp, calculating presence who understands the true price of power. Roy has quietly built one of the more interesting OTT careers of her generation, and she clearly relishes a character with more going on beneath the surface than the trailer lets on.

The ensemble runs deep — Nimrit Kaur Ahluwalia, Harman Singha and Aasheema Vardaan round out a Punjab-soaked world directed by Divyanshu Malhotra and co-written by a four-person team including Faizal Akhtar and Radhika Anand. The visual grammar is moody and fast-cut, all sodium-lit highways and interiors thick with unspoken debt. It looks less like a glossy streaming product and more like the gritty regional noir the platform has been quietly getting good at.

For the diaspora specifically, this one cuts close. The Punjabi migration story is the diaspora story for huge swaths of the community in Canada, the UK and the US — and the dark underbelly of that journey, the predatory agents and the families left holding the loss, rarely gets dramatised with this much intent. Ab Hoga Hisaab isn't subtle about its politics, and it doesn't need to be. The fear is real, the casting is sharp, and the central question — what do you do when the system that promised you a future eats your family instead — is one a lot of households have lived a quieter version of.

It's free, it's eight episodes of revenge-thriller momentum, and it's built on the one anxiety the diaspora can't look away from. Stream it on MX Player from June 18, and don't be surprised if it's the family group chat's most-discussed show of the week.
